glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: God breaks the spiritual silence by calling Samuel, revealing His word, and establishing him as a trustworthy prophet.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Samuel serves under Eli at Shiloh when the word of the LORD is rare. The judgment already announced against Eli’s house forms the background to the LORD’s call to Samuel.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• 1 Samuel 3:1–10 — The LORD Calls Samuel

  • 1 Samuel 3:11–14 — The Word Against Eli’s House

  • 1 Samuel 3:15–18 — Samuel Tells Eli Everything

  • 1 Samuel 3:19–21 — Samuel Established as a Prophet of the LORD

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Then the LORD appeared again in Shiloh. For the LORD revealed Himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the LORD.” (1 Samuel 3:21, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The chapter shows that hearing God requires responsiveness, and that God’s word will stand even when it brings difficult truth and judgment.

1 Samuel 3 marks a major transition in the spiritual life of Israel. The chapter opens by saying that “the word of the LORD was rare in those days” and that there was no widespread revelation. Against that background, God begins speaking to Samuel. Eli’s leadership is fading, and judgment hangs over his household.

Samuel is still young and serving under Eli when the LORD calls him during the night. At first Samuel assumes that Eli is calling him. After the third time, Eli realizes that the LORD is speaking and instructs Samuel to respond, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears.” God then gives Samuel a difficult message concerning the judgment of Eli’s house.

Samuel is afraid to tell Eli what he has heard, but Eli insists that he speak honestly. Samuel tells him everything and hides nothing. Eli receives the message with the acknowledgment that the LORD is God and will do what seems good to Him. Samuel’s first message requires him to speak faithfully even when the truth is painful or costly to deliver.

The chapter closes by showing that Samuel continues to grow, that the LORD is with him, and that none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground. All Israel recognizes that Samuel has been established as a prophet of the LORD. God’s word, rare at the beginning of the chapter, is now being revealed through Samuel. When God restores His word among His people, He calls servants to hear, obey, and speak faithfully.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Samuel 3:1–10 — The LORD Calls Samuel

The LORD calls Samuel repeatedly while he serves under Eli, and Eli eventually recognizes who is calling. When the LORD comes and stands and calls again, Samuel answers as a servant ready to hear.

1 Samuel 3:11–14 — The Word Against Eli’s House

The LORD confirms the judgment already announced against Eli’s house, because Eli knew his sons’ iniquity and did not restrain them. He swears that its iniquity will not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.

1 Samuel 3:15–18 — Samuel Tells Eli Everything

Samuel is afraid to tell Eli the vision, but at Eli’s insistence he reports everything and hides nothing. Eli acknowledges the LORD’s right to do what seems good to Him.

1 Samuel 3:19–21 — Samuel Established as a Prophet of the LORD

The LORD is with Samuel and confirms his words, so that all Israel recognizes him as an established prophet. The LORD continues revealing Himself to Samuel at Shiloh by His word.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
1 Samuel 3 explains how Samuel moves from being a child serving in the sanctuary to being recognized as a prophet of God. His calling is not based on human appointment, family position, or personal ambition. God Himself calls him, speaks to him, and confirms his ministry.

The chapter also shows the importance of receiving and speaking God’s word faithfully. Samuel’s first prophetic assignment is not easy or flattering. He must carry a message of judgment to the very man who has helped raise him. His willingness to tell Eli everything demonstrates the kind of faithfulness that will characterize his prophetic ministry.

This chapter also continues the contrast between old and new spiritual leadership. Eli’s house is moving toward judgment, while Samuel is being established by God. Yet the emphasis is not simply on replacing one leader with another. The deeper issue is the restoration of God’s word among His people.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The Word of the LORD
The chapter begins with the word of the LORD being rare and ends with the LORD revealing Himself again through His word. This creates the main movement of the chapter.

God Calls Personally
Samuel’s prophetic ministry begins with God calling him by name. His service becomes rooted in a personal response to God’s initiative.

Learning to Hear God
Samuel does not immediately understand what is happening. Recognition develops through repeated calling, Eli’s guidance, and Samuel’s willingness to respond.

Servant-Hearted Response
“Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears” expresses readiness, humility, and submission. Samuel does not ask God to speak on his terms but presents himself as one who is ready to listen and obey.

The Seriousness of God’s Word
The first message Samuel receives is difficult. God’s revelation is not given merely to encourage but also to confront sin and announce judgment when necessary.

Faithful Delivery of the Message
Samuel is afraid, but he does not alter or conceal what God has spoken. His faithfulness becomes part of the evidence that God is establishing him as a prophet.

God’s Presence with Samuel
“The LORD was with him” explains the effectiveness and credibility of Samuel’s growing ministry.

A Prophet Established by God
Samuel’s authority is confirmed because God stands behind his words. Israel recognizes what God has already done.

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The word of the LORD was rare
This means that direct divine revelation was uncommon during that period. The phrase reflects Israel’s spiritual decline and prepares for the significance of Samuel’s prophetic calling.

There was no widespread revelation
Public prophetic revelation was not occurring regularly throughout Israel. The chapter presents Samuel’s calling as part of a renewal of God’s revealed word.

The lamp of God
This most naturally refers to the sanctuary lamp, which was to remain burning through the night. The statement also fits the larger movement of the chapter: although spiritual conditions are dark, God’s presence and purposes have not been extinguished.

Samuel did not yet know the LORD
This does not necessarily mean Samuel had no relationship with God at all. The following clause clarifies the sense: “nor was the word of the LORD yet revealed to him” (3:7).

Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears
Samuel identifies himself as a servant ready to receive God’s word. “Hears” includes the idea of attentive listening with readiness to obey.

Both ears of everyone who hears it will tingle
This Hebrew expression describes news so shocking and severe that those who hear it will react with alarm.

I will judge his house forever
God confirms the judgment already announced in chapter 2. Eli’s family will lose its privileged priestly standing because of persistent sin and dishonor toward God.

His sons made themselves vile
Eli’s sons knowingly acted in ways that brought guilt and disgrace upon themselves and upon their priestly office.

He did not restrain them
Eli rebuked his sons verbally, but he failed to exercise the authority necessary to stop their continued corruption. His failure was therefore not complete silence but inadequate action.

Did not let any of his words fall to the ground
The expression means that Samuel’s prophetic words proved reliable and effective because God fulfilled what He spoke through him.

Established as a prophet of the LORD
Samuel’s prophetic role becomes publicly recognized throughout Israel. His authority rests on God’s calling and confirmation.

From Dan to Beersheba
This common expression refers to the full extent of Israel from north to south. It emphasizes that Samuel’s recognition as a prophet became national.

The LORD revealed Himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the LORD
The chapter ends by showing that God’s renewed revelation continues. Samuel becomes the means through whom God again makes His word known to Israel.

culture.title: Presence Driven
culture.statement:
Culture Statement
Holy Spirit is God Himself dwelling within us. He directs our decisions, shapes our communities, and equips us to supernaturally impact our surroundings. We hear, connect, and obey as He leads. We are Spirit-led and unashamed.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 3
culture.html:
Living It in 1 Samuel 3
“The LORD was with him” (1 Samuel 3:19). The defining reality behind Samuel’s growing ministry was not his position, ability, or reputation, but the presence of God with him. The Lord’s presence gave weight to his words and effectiveness to his calling.

We want the same reality to characterize us. We do not want merely to do things for God or depend upon programs, personalities, methods, or human ability. We want to live and serve with the Lord present among us, directing and empowering what we do.

culture.title: Hear God and Obey
culture.statement:
Culture Statement
East Gate exists to teach people how to hear God’s voice, connect with Him daily, and walk with Him in obedience.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 3
culture.html:
Living It in 1 Samuel 3
“Speak, for Your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10). Samuel positioned himself to hear God, but hearing was only the beginning. He had to receive what God said, connect it to the situation before him, and then obey even when obedience was difficult.

This is the pattern we want to live: hear, connect, and obey. We listen for what God is saying, connect His truth to our lives and circumstances, and respond to what He shows us. Hearing God is not merely about receiving revelation. The goal is a life that walks with Him in obedience.

culture.title: Hear God and Obey
culture.statement:
Culture Statement
East Gate exists to teach people how to hear God’s voice, connect with Him daily, and walk with Him in obedience.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 3
culture.html:
Living It in 1 Samuel 3
“Then the LORD appeared again in Shiloh” (1 Samuel 3:21). The word “again” is significant. Samuel’s first encounter with God was not intended to be his last. As he continued before the Lord, God continued revealing Himself to him.

We can position ourselves to hear God with expectancy, but we must also “take heed how you hear” (Luke 8:18). Hearing God is a privilege that carries responsibility. Jesus said, “For everyone to whom much is given, from him much will be required” (Luke 12:48). The more God entrusts to us, the more carefully we must steward what we hear. We want to expect God to speak and be ready to obey when He does.

culture.title: People of the Word
culture.statement:
Culture Statement
The Holy Bible is the only infallible and final authority for Christian faith and life. The Holy Scriptures are timeless, inerrant and are to be read personally, discerned corporately, and walked out in community. We interpret all Scripture through the life and teachings of Jesus, trusting Holy Spirit to reveal truth and transform us as we submit ourselves fully to God’s revealed Word.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 3
culture.html:
Living It in 1 Samuel 3
“Then Samuel told him everything, and hid nothing from him” (1 Samuel 3:18). Samuel was afraid to tell Eli what God had said, but he did not soften the message, leave out the difficult parts, or change it to make it easier to receive.

As People of the Word, we do not water down Scripture because something is uncomfortable, unpopular, or difficult to communicate. We submit ourselves to what God has revealed rather than reshaping His Word around our preferences. Samuel also reminds us that faithfulness does not require harshness. He cared about Eli and felt the weight of the message, but he still told him everything. We want to handle God’s Word with the same courage, humility, accuracy, and integrity.

sections.title: Samuel Established as a Prophet of the LORD

1.brief: The boy Samuel ministers to the LORD before Eli at a time when the word of the LORD was rare and there was no widespread revelation. This scarcity of God’s word sets the scene for His call to Samuel.
1.explain:
“Now the boy Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli.”

Chapter 3 opens with Samuel at his post. “The boy” translates a word that covers a wide range of ages, from a small child to a young man. Samuel had been growing up at the sanctuary since he was weaned (1:24), so he was no longer a small child, but Scripture does not give his age. He “ministered to the LORD,” serving as an attendant at the sanctuary, as he had been doing since he was left at Shiloh (2:11, 18). His service was “to the LORD,” because God was the One he served, and “before Eli,” under the old priest's oversight.

“And the word of the LORD was rare in those days;”

The narrator describes the spiritual condition of Israel. “The word of the LORD” means a message God Himself speaks, usually through a prophet. It “was rare” in those days. The Hebrew word also means precious or costly; something scarce becomes precious. God had not gone completely silent, since a man of God had recently brought a message to Eli (2:27–36), but such messages were unusual. “Those days” were the closing years of the judges, when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25), and the priesthood at Shiloh was corrupt. Scripture does not give a reason for the scarcity here. Elsewhere, God's silence often accompanies a people's turning away from Him. Years later, when Saul had rejected God's word, “the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams or by Urim or by the prophets” (28:6).

“there was no widespread revelation.”

“Revelation” refers to a prophetic vision, the kind of revelation God gave to prophets. In those days a prophet was called a “seer” (9:9), because he saw what God showed him. “Widespread” carries the idea of breaking out or spreading abroad. Visions were not breaking through to the people. This scarcity of God's word sets the scene for His call to Samuel. By the end of the chapter, God's word will again be known throughout Israel (3:19–21).
1.notes:
“Revelation” translates the Hebrew word hazon, ‘vision,’ a word used for prophetic revelation from God. The same Hebrew word stands behind “revelation” in Proverbs 29:18: “Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint.”

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century AD, said Samuel began to prophesy at twelve. That figure is tradition, not Scripture, and cannot be confirmed.

The details of the chapter suggest a boy old enough to carry out sanctuary duties such as opening the doors (3:15) and to understand and repeat a complex message (3:18).

2.brief: At that time Eli is lying down in his place, his eyes having grown so dim that he cannot see. His failing sight marks Eli’s age and pictures the spiritual dimness of his leadership, since he had not stopped the corruption in his own household.
2.explain:
“And it came to pass at that time,”

This phrase places the night's events in the time when the LORD's word was rare. Nothing yet suggested that God was about to speak.

“while Eli was lying down in his place,”

Eli was resting “in his place,” where he usually slept. The verse does not say where that was, but it was near enough to Samuel that the boy could hear a voice in the night, assume Eli had called, and run to him (3:5). The call came while the household was asleep.

“and when his eyes had begun to grow so dim that he could not see,”

Eli's eyesight was failing with age. “Had begun” shows that it was still getting worse. By the time of his death he would be completely blind (4:15). A man in that condition depended on others, especially at night, which helps explain why Samuel ran to him so quickly. Eli's failing sight also pictures the spiritual dimness of his leadership. He had misread Hannah's prayer (1:13–14) and had not stopped the corruption in his own household (2:22–25). The narrator presents his blindness as a physical condition, but it fits a priest who could no longer see clearly in body or in leadership. God was about to speak to the boy instead.
2.notes: The Hebrew word behind “grow so dim” means faint or dim and comes from a verb meaning to grow weak or dim. It differs from the Hebrew expression in 4:15, literally ‘his eyes stood,’ that is, they were fixed and no longer saw.

3.brief: Before the lamp of God goes out in the tabernacle of the LORD, where the ark of God is, Samuel is lying down. The scene is set late in the night within the sanctuary, though the text does not place Samuel in the Most Holy Place or beside the ark.
3.explain:
“and before the lamp of God went out”

The time was late at night. “The lamp of God” was the golden lampstand in the Holy Place of the tabernacle. God commanded that it burn with pure olive oil and that the priests tend it “from evening until morning before the LORD” (Exodus 27:21). It burned through the night. The fact that it had not yet gone out means that it was still dark, probably in the hours before dawn. When morning came, Samuel would open the doors of the house of the LORD (3:15). Israel's spiritual life was dim, God's word was rare, and the high priest's eyes were failing, but the lamp in God's house was still burning.

“in the tabernacle of the LORD”

The scene was “the tabernacle of the LORD,” the sanctuary at Shiloh. The Hebrew word here means a temple or palace, as in 1:9.

“where the ark of God was,”

The narrator identifies the sanctuary as the place “where the ark of God was.” The ark, which held the tablets of the law and over which the LORD was enthroned between the cherubim (4:4), was kept in the Most Holy Place. Its mention prepares for the next chapter, where the ark will be carried into battle and captured.

“and while Samuel was lying down,”

“Samuel was lying down,” asleep within the sanctuary precincts. The text does not say exactly where he slept. The language describes the sanctuary complex broadly. It does not mean that Samuel slept inside the Most Holy Place or beside the ark; that inner room was entered only by the high priest, once a year (Leviticus 16:2, 34). Samuel served and slept within the sanctuary precincts without entering the restricted areas reserved for priestly ministry. His precise sleeping location is not identified.

4.brief: The LORD calls Samuel, and the boy answers at once, “Here I am!” God breaks the silence of those days by addressing a young servant by name.
4.explain:
“that the LORD called Samuel.”

Into the silence of those days, “the LORD called Samuel.” God broke the scarcity of His word by speaking to a boy. He addressed Samuel by name. The call came not to the high priest or to his sons, but to the young servant faithfully lying in his place.

“And he answered, ‘Here I am!’”

Samuel answered at once: “Here I am!” The words express readiness and availability. They are the same words Abraham spoke when God called him (Genesis 22:1), the same words Moses spoke at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4), and the response Isaiah gave when he heard the Lord's voice (“Here am I! Send me,” Isaiah 6:8). Samuel did not yet know who was calling, but his response was the response of a servant ready to answer.
4.notes:
The Hebrew text reads “the LORD called Samuel.” The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads ‘the Lord called, Samuel, Samuel,’ anticipating 3:10. The NKJV follows the Hebrew.

Samuel's answer “Here I am” translates the single Hebrew word hinneni, literally ‘behold me.’ The same word recurs in Samuel's answers to Eli in 3:5, 6, 8, and 16.

5.brief: Samuel runs to Eli, thinking the old priest has called him, but Eli says he did not call and sends him back to lie down. Samuel’s readiness is clear, though he does not yet recognize whose voice he has heard.
5.explain:
“So he ran to Eli and said, ‘Here I am, for you called me.’”

Samuel “ran to Eli.” He assumed the old priest, who could not see, had called him for help. His running shows eager readiness to serve. “You called me” reveals his misunderstanding: he did not yet recognize the LORD's voice.

“And he said, ‘I did not call; lie down again.’”

Eli had not called. He told Samuel to “lie down again.” At this point Eli did not yet understand what was happening either.

“And he went and lay down.”

Samuel obeyed. He returned and lay down. Samuel's readiness is clear, though he did not yet recognize whose voice he had heard.

6.brief: The LORD calls Samuel a second time, and again Samuel goes to Eli, who calls him my son and sends him back. The repeated call shows the LORD’s patience while Samuel still misunderstands.
6.explain:
“Then the LORD called yet again, ‘Samuel!’”

The LORD called a second time. “Yet again” emphasizes God's persistence. He did not give up when Samuel misunderstood.

“So Samuel arose and went to Eli, and said, ‘Here I am, for you called me.’”

Samuel again went to Eli with the same words. He still did not recognize the voice.

“He answered, ‘I did not call, my son; lie down again.’”

Eli again denied calling. This time he called Samuel “my son,” a warm, fatherly address. The repeated call shows the LORD's patience while Samuel still misunderstood. God was willing to call again and again until His servant learned to recognize His voice.

7.brief: The narrator explains that Samuel did not yet know the LORD, because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him. This does not mean Samuel was ungodly like Eli’s sons, who “did not know the LORD” (2:12), but that he had not yet experienced God speaking to him personally.
7.explain:
“(Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD,”

The narrator pauses to explain why Samuel did not recognize the voice. “Samuel did not yet know the LORD.” This does not mean Samuel was ungodly, lacked faith, or had no relationship with God. He had been faithfully ministering to the LORD for years (2:18; 3:1), and he grew in favor with the LORD (2:26). The difference with Eli's sons is significant. They “did not know the LORD” because of their wickedness and disregard for Him (2:12). Samuel did not yet know the LORD in the specific sense explained in the next clause.

“nor was the word of the LORD yet revealed to him.)”

The second clause clarifies the first. “The word of the LORD” had not yet been “revealed to him.” Samuel had not yet personally experienced God speaking to him through prophetic revelation. He knew about the LORD and served Him, but he had not yet heard His voice. That is why he mistook God's call for Eli's. He was about to learn.
7.notes: The Hebrew word translated “yet,” meaning ‘not yet’ or ‘before,’ appears twice in this verse: Samuel “did not yet know the LORD,” and the word of the LORD was not “yet revealed to him.” The repetition signals that this condition was about to change.

8.brief: When the LORD calls the third time and Samuel again comes to him, Eli perceives that the LORD has been calling the boy. Despite his failures, Eli recognizes God’s work and is able to guide Samuel.
8.explain:
“And the LORD called Samuel again the third time.”

God called a third time. The repetition shows His patient persistence.

“So he arose and went to Eli, and said, ‘Here I am, for you did call me.’”

Samuel again went to Eli, this time insisting, “you did call me.” He was sure he had heard someone call.

“Then Eli perceived that the LORD had called the boy.”

Finally “Eli perceived” what was happening. “The LORD had called the boy.” Despite his failures, Eli recognized God's work and was able to guide Samuel. The old priest, whose eyes were dim and whose house was under judgment, still understood enough to recognize the LORD's call. His discernment here balances his earlier misjudgment of Hannah (1:13–14).

9.brief: Eli tells Samuel to lie down and, if he is called again, to answer, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears.” His instruction prepares Samuel to respond as a servant ready to listen and obey.
9.explain:
“Therefore Eli said to Samuel, ‘Go, lie down;’”

Eli instructed Samuel to return to his place.

“and it shall be, if He calls you, that you must say, ‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears.’”

Eli taught Samuel how to respond. If the voice called again, Samuel should say, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant hears.” The words express a servant's readiness to listen and obey. “Speak” invites God to communicate. “Your servant” acknowledges God as Master. “Hears” means not only listening but heeding, being ready to obey. His instruction prepared Samuel to respond as a servant ready to listen and obey.

“So Samuel went and lay down in his place.”

Samuel obeyed and returned to his place. He now waited, knowing that the voice might be the LORD's.
9.notes: “Hears” translates the Hebrew verb shama', which means to hear, listen, heed, or obey. The same Hebrew verb is translated “obey” in 15:22: “to obey is better than sacrifice.”

10.brief: The LORD comes and stands and calls as at the other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” and Samuel answers, “Speak, for Your servant hears.” The LORD’s coming is a real divine manifestation, though the text does not describe what Samuel saw, and Samuel now answers Him directly.
10.explain:
“Now the LORD came and stood”

This time something more happened. “The LORD came and stood.” God's coming and standing describes a genuine divine manifestation, not merely Samuel imagining or sensing a message. The LORD was personally present. The text does not specify whether Samuel saw a visible form. Scripture describes similar moments, such as when “the LORD descended in the cloud and stood with” Moses (Exodus 34:5). Here it simply affirms the reality of God's presence without describing what Samuel saw.

“and called as at other times, ‘Samuel! Samuel!’”

God called “as at other times,” but now He called the name twice: “Samuel! Samuel!” A double call appears at other significant moments in Scripture, as when God called “Abraham, Abraham!” (Genesis 22:11) and “Moses, Moses!” (Exodus 3:4). It expresses urgency and personal address.

“And Samuel answered, ‘Speak, for Your servant hears.’”

Samuel answered as Eli had taught him, with one difference. He said, “Speak, for Your servant hears,” without the word ‘LORD.’ The reason is not given. He may have been overwhelmed, or simply abbreviated the words. What matters is that Samuel now answered God directly, as a servant ready to hear and obey.

11.brief: The LORD tells Samuel that He is about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears it tingle. Samuel’s first revelation is a word of coming judgment.
11.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Samuel:”

God's first message to Samuel begins.

“Behold, I will do something in Israel”

“Behold” calls for attention. God was about to act “in Israel,” among His own people.

“at which both ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.”

The event would be so shocking that “both ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.” The image describes news so terrible that it makes the ears ring with horror. The same expression is used later for the disaster on Jerusalem in Manasseh's day (2 Kings 21:12) and in Jeremiah's day (Jeremiah 19:3). Samuel's first revelation is a word of coming judgment. The boy who had been waiting to hear God would first hear of catastrophe.

12.brief: In that day the LORD will carry out against Eli everything He has spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end. The word Samuel receives confirms the warning already delivered by the man of God (2:27–36).
12.explain:
“In that day I will perform against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house,”

God would “perform,” carry out, everything He had said “against Eli” and “concerning his house.” The word Samuel received confirms the warning already delivered by the man of God (2:27–36). God's word would not fail.

“from beginning to end.”

The judgment would be complete, “from beginning to end.” Nothing God had said would be left unfulfilled. The sign of the sons' deaths (2:34) and the long-term judgment on Eli's descendants (2:31–33) would all come to pass.

13.brief: The LORD has told Eli that He will judge his house forever for the iniquity Eli knew about: his sons made themselves vile, and he did not restrain them. Eli had rebuked them, but he failed to stop their wickedness or remove them from their priestly service.
13.explain:
“For I have told him that I will judge his house forever”

God had already “told” Eli through the man of God (2:27–36). The judgment on his house would be permanent: “forever.”

“for the iniquity which he knows,”

The judgment was “for the iniquity which he knows.” Eli was not ignorant. He knew what his sons were doing (2:22–24).

“because his sons made themselves vile,”

The sons “made themselves vile.” They brought contempt and curse upon themselves through their conduct.

“and he did not restrain them.”

The charge against Eli is that “he did not restrain them.” Eli had verbally confronted his sons (2:23–25), so this does not mean he never rebuked them. His failure was that he did not effectively stop their wickedness or remove them from their priestly service. As high priest he had the authority to do so. His words were not matched by action. A rebuke without consequence left the abuse in place.
13.notes:
The Hebrew phrase translated “made themselves vile” (meqallelim lahem) is unusual. An ancient Jewish scribal tradition lists this verse among places where the scribes altered the text out of reverence.

The Septuagint reads that Eli's sons ‘spoke evil against God’ (Brenton's English translation of the Septuagint), which fits the scribal tradition mentioned above. In Hebrew the word for ‘God’ looks much like lahem, the word rendered ‘themselves.’ On that reading, the sons' sin was blasphemy against God, as the ESV renders it. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV reads “made themselves vile.”

“Restrain” translates a rare Hebrew verb used with this sense only here. Hebrew lexicons give ‘rebuke,’ though the meaning is uncertain, and the Septuagint has ‘admonish.’ English versions vary between ‘restrain’ (KJV, NKJV, ESV) and ‘rebuke’ (NASB).

The word alone does not prove whether stopping or rebuking is meant. The judgment that Eli failed to act effectively comes from the context, since he did rebuke his sons with words (2:23–25) and is still held responsible.

14.brief: The LORD has sworn to the house of Eli that its iniquity will not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever. This oath makes the judgment on Eli’s house irrevocable; it does not teach that forgiveness is closed to everyone who has sinned grievously.
14.explain:
“And therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli”

God had “sworn,” making an oath that could not be revoked. The judgment was certain.

“that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever.”

The iniquity of Eli's house would “not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever.” The very sacrifices and offerings that Eli's sons had despised could not cover their sin. This oath makes the judgment on Eli's house irrevocable. It does not teach that forgiveness is closed to everyone who has sinned grievously. It is a specific judgment on a specific priestly house that had persistently treated God's offerings with contempt.

15.brief: Samuel lies down until morning and then opens the doors of the house of the LORD, continuing his ordinary duties. He is afraid to tell Eli the vision he has received.
15.explain:
“So Samuel lay down until morning,”

Samuel lay awake, perhaps, until morning. The night's message must have weighed on him.

“and opened the doors of the house of the LORD.”

When morning came, Samuel “opened the doors of the house of the LORD.” He continued his ordinary duties. The boy who had just received God's word went about his daily work. His faithfulness in ordinary service had prepared him to hear God, and hearing God did not release him from ordinary service.

“And Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision.”

“Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision.” The message concerned Eli, the man who had raised him. Samuel feared telling him that God had pronounced judgment on his house. “Vision” here describes the revelation he had received, whether seen or heard. His fear was understandable. He was a boy, and the message was devastating.
15.notes: “Vision” translates the Hebrew word mar'ah, a word for a vision as one of the ways God reveals Himself. The same Hebrew word appears in Numbers 12:6, where God says He makes Himself known to a prophet “in a vision.”

16.brief: Eli calls him, “Samuel, my son!” and Samuel answers, “Here I am.” The same readiness Samuel showed when he was called in the night now meets the hard task of facing Eli.
16.explain:
“Then Eli called Samuel and said, ‘Samuel, my son!’”

Eli called for Samuel. The voice calling “Samuel” now was Eli's. He called him “my son,” with warmth and perhaps apprehension.

“He answered, ‘Here I am.’”

Samuel answered with the same words he had spoken to the LORD and to Eli in the night: “Here I am.” The same readiness Samuel showed when he was called in the night now met the hard task of facing Eli.

17.brief: Eli asks what the LORD has spoken and binds Samuel with a solemn oath not to hide anything from him. Eli insists on hearing the full word, however painful it may be.
17.explain:
“And he said, ‘What is the word that the LORD spoke to you?’”

Eli asked directly. He knew that the LORD had spoken to Samuel.

“Please do not hide it from me.”

Eli asked Samuel not to hold anything back. He suspected the message concerned him.

“God do so to you, and more also, if you hide anything from me of all the things that He said to you.”

Eli bound Samuel with a solemn oath. “God do so to you, and more also” was a common oath formula calling down God's judgment if the person failed to do what was required. Eli insisted on hearing the full word, however painful it might be. He would not allow Samuel to soften or withhold the message.
17.notes: The oath formula also appears in 1 Samuel 14:44; 20:13; and 25:22. The penalty invoked by the formula is left unstated.

18.brief: Samuel tells Eli everything and hides nothing, and Eli responds, “It is the LORD. Let Him do what seems good to Him.” Samuel proves a faithful messenger, and Eli submits to the LORD’s judgment, though his submission does not undo his earlier failure.
18.explain:
“Then Samuel told him everything, and hid nothing from him.”

Samuel obeyed. He “told him everything, and hid nothing.” Samuel proved a faithful messenger. His first task as God's prophet was to deliver a hard word to the man he served, and he did it completely. This faithfulness in delivering God's word would mark his whole ministry.

“And he said, ‘It is the LORD. Let Him do what seems good to Him.’”

Eli responded with submission. “It is the LORD” acknowledged that the message came from God. “Let Him do what seems good to Him” accepted God's right to judge. Eli submitted to the LORD's judgment, though his submission did not undo his earlier failure. He accepted the verdict, but he did not repent by removing his sons from office, and the judgment would come as God had said.

19.brief: Samuel grows, and the LORD is with him and lets none of his words fall to the ground. God Himself confirms Samuel’s words by bringing them to pass.
19.explain:
“So Samuel grew,”

Samuel continued to grow, physically and in his role as God's servant.

“and the LORD was with him”

“The LORD was with him.” This phrase marks God's favor and presence. It will be used later of David (18:12, 14). God's presence with Samuel was the source of his authority.

“and let none of his words fall to the ground.”

“None of his words” fell “to the ground.” The image is of words that fail, dropping uselessly. God confirmed Samuel's words by bringing them to pass. When Samuel spoke for God, what he said happened. This was the test of a true prophet in the Law: if a prophet's word does not come to pass, “that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22). God Himself confirmed Samuel's words by bringing them to pass.
19.notes: In Hebrew, the image of the LORD letting none of Samuel's words “fall to the ground” uses the same verb that the NKJV translates “failed” in Joshua 21:45: “Not a word failed of any good thing which the LORD had spoken to the house of Israel.”

20.brief: All Israel, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, knows that Samuel has been established as a prophet of the LORD. His recognition as God’s prophet becomes national.
20.explain:
“And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew”

Samuel's reputation spread throughout the nation. “From Dan to Beersheba” describes all Israel from the northern border (Dan) to the southern border (Beersheba). The phrase became the standard way of saying ‘the whole land’ (compare 2 Samuel 24:2).

“that Samuel had been established as a prophet of the LORD.”

All Israel “knew that Samuel had been established as a prophet of the LORD.” “Established” means confirmed or proven trustworthy. The word is related to the word “sure” in 2:35 (“a sure house”). Samuel was recognized as a true prophet. His recognition as God's prophet became national. After years when the word of the LORD was rare, Israel again had a prophet.

21.brief: The LORD appears again in Shiloh and reveals Himself to Samuel there by the word of the LORD. The chapter that began with God’s word rare now ends with His word being revealed again.
21.explain:
“Then the LORD appeared again in Shiloh.”

The chapter ends with God's continued presence. “The LORD appeared again in Shiloh.” God did not speak to Samuel only once. He continued to reveal Himself at Shiloh.

“For the LORD revealed Himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the LORD.”

The way God revealed Himself was “by the word of the LORD.” His self-revelation came through His spoken word to Samuel. The chapter that began with God's word rare (3:1) now ends with His word being revealed again. The LORD had broken the silence. Through the boy who had learned to say, “Speak, for Your servant hears,” God's word would again reach His people. The opening clause of 4:1 continues the thought: “And the word of Samuel came to all Israel.”
21.notes: The Septuagint adds at the end of this verse that Samuel was trusted to be a prophet from one end of the land to the other, and that Eli was very old and his sons continued to act wickedly. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV is shorter.
